passage:
Sunday night, can't sleep.
It's been three weeks since I reported the billing error. Since then my manager barely looks at me. Tuesday's team lunch: everyone moved their chairs a little, and the chat stopped when I sat down. Nobody has said a word about it. Feels like I'm being punished for doing the right thing. I keep thinking, was it worth it? Today I did something. I started a notes file with dates: the meeting my manager cancelled, the project I was moved off, the silence. Then I rang Sahil, who listened for an hour and reminded me that I had reported a real problem. He said integrity costs something, but it's still worth something. I'm going to book a session with the union rep tomorrow. I'm hurt, and I'm not going to stay silent about it.

qa.q: How long ago did the diary writer report the billing error?
How does the diary writer feel about the reactions at work?
qa.a: Punished for doing the right thing, and hurt and doubtful about whether it was worth it.

qa.q: What did the diary writer do to protect against retaliation?
qa.a: Started a dated notes file of what changed, called Sahil for support and planned to see the union rep.

qa.q: How might the manager see the report of the billing error?
qa.a: The manager may have taken it as criticism or embarrassment, which could explain the cold shoulder, though it doesn't excuse it.

grounding: After reporting an issue the protagonist is shunned and feels punished; documenting retaliation, leaning on outside support and valuing integrity's cost.

passage:
The pathology lab at the private hospital used to feel like a second home. Then Parul reported that expired reagents were being used on patient samples, first to her boss, then in writing to the quality officer when nothing changed. The quality officer, Dr Mathew, thanked her, took copies, and opened an inquiry that same week.

Since then, her boss hadn't said good morning. Her night shifts had doubled. At lunch, colleagues went quiet when she sat down.

Parul started a notebook: dates, shift changes, remarks. She sent Dr Mathew a short update each Friday.

On Sunday she met Aparna, her friend from nursing college, at a tea shop. "I feel like I'm being punished for doing right," Parul said. Aparna held her hand. "You are. And you still did right. Keep the notebook. Come to my place on your off days."

Parul went home lighter, though not lighter enough.

qa.a: Parul reported that expired reagents were being used on patient samples.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after her colleagues went quiet?
qa.a: Parul felt betrayed and punished, as if she was being made to pay for doing the right thing.

qa.q: What steps is Parul taking to protect herself?
qa.a: Parul keeps a notebook of dates and shift changes, updates the quality officer weekly, and leans on Aparna outside work.

qa.q: How does Aparna see what Parul did?
qa.a: Aparna sees it as right, even though it has cost Parul, and offers comfort and a place to rest.

grounding: The scene shows a young woman frozen out after reporting wrongdoing, documenting retaliation and leaning on outside support.

passage:
Dear Vishal sir,

You were my manager at my first internship, and you once said I could write if things got hard. They have.

Three months ago I reported that our site supervisor was signing off safety checks without doing them. I told the compliance officer, who thanked me, met me twice, and has started an inquiry. I thought I'd done the right thing.

Since then my boss has taken me off the main project. Colleagues who used to share lunch now eat at another table. Nobody says it's because of the report, but I feel it every day, like being punished for telling the truth.

I've started writing down each change with the date, like you taught us to document everything. I've also joined a professional engineers' group that meets on Saturdays; two of them have been through this.

I don't regret it. But it's lonely. Could we talk on the phone this weekend?

Uday

qa.q: What was the site supervisor doing without checks?
qa.a: The site supervisor was signing off safety checks without doing them.

qa.q: How does Uday feel since the report?
qa.a: Uday feels punished and lonely, as if being made to pay for telling the truth, but does not regret it.

qa.q: What wise steps is Uday taking?
qa.a: Uday documents each change with dates, joins an outside professional group and reaches out to a trusted former manager.

qa.q: How might the colleagues who moved tables see Uday?
qa.a: They may fear being linked to the report or the boss's anger, so they keep their distance even if some agree with Uday.

grounding: The letter shows a young employee frozen out after reporting wrongdoing, documenting retaliation and leaning on outside support.
